01 · The question · 0:00–0:40

Where should a Harvard student study?

The answer depends on the task—and students need better information than a single ranking.

Say: “Harvard students choose among many library spaces, but the best space for silent reading may be a poor choice for a team presentation. I built a decision tool around that practical choice.”

103

spaces compared

Across 13 Harvard libraries, representing 2,098 listed seats.

02 · The data · 0:40–1:25

One official census.

Every record returned by Harvard Library’s public space finder: 45 fields covering capacity, noise, location, reservation, images, and 19 amenities.

Say: “I downloaded all 103 room records from Harvard Library’s public API on September 21, 2026 and joined them to official library metadata. A one means explicitly listed. A zero means not listed—not confirmed absent.”

Unit of analysis

One named room or study area.

Safety

No names, contact details, health information, precise personal locations, or behavioral histories.

03 · The tool · 1:25–2:15

Four presets—or your priorities.

Eight visible sliders change the ranking, and the comparison view shows why spaces trade places.

Say: “The dashboard translates published fields into eight facility signals, then applies transparent weights. Students can use a task preset or adjust every priority. The score is a fit model, not a student rating.”

Deep-focus preset

Quiet30

04 · Findings · 2:15–3:20

Capacity and task are uneven.

Lamont and Widener hold 47% of listed seats, while more than half of records are coded Chatter.

Say: “Three findings stand out. Lamont and Widener account for 992 of 2,098 seats. Fifty-eight spaces are coded Chatter versus 45 Silent or Whispers. And collaboration equipment is selective: 32 spaces list displays and 27 list whiteboards.”

58

spaces coded Chatter

The best choice depends on what the student needs to do.

05 · Recommendations · 3:20–4:20

Use the inventory to target action.

The data identifies what to verify next rather than pretending to measure student experience directly.

Say: “First, protect and clearly label lower-noise capacity. Second, verify equipment in reservable rooms and prioritize collaboration upgrades. Third, add anonymous occupancy counts and a short feature-priority survey.”

  1. Protect quiet zones and standardize wayfinding.
  2. Target upgrades after verifying displays and whiteboards.
  3. Measure demand anonymously by broad time block.

06 · Limits & close · 4:20–5:00

A decision aid, not a verdict.

The project supports comparison and facilities planning. It cannot prove satisfaction, crowding, or academic outcomes.

Say: “The data covers every API record but not every place students study. Richer documentation can also create higher scores. The next version should add anonymous occupancy snapshots and student preference data. For now, the dashboard makes the evidence and its limits visible.”

Best next dataset

Anonymous seat counts by broad time block + short feature-priority survey.
